newsitem.title: UK: Britain warns of extra cancer risk from ozone loss.
newsitem.headline: Britain warns of extra cancer risk from ozone loss.

text.p: The risk of developing skin cancer in Britain has risen by as much as 10 percent because damage to the ozone layer from CFCs and other chemicals is letting through more ultraviolet radiation, the government said on Wednesday.

The Department of the Environment said record damage to the ozone layer over Britain in the past 12 months could result in increased exposure to ultraviolet (UV) radiation with potentially harmful effects on health, air quality and crops.
It can cause sunburn and skin cancer as well as damage the eyes and the immune system.

"Current and projected levels of ozone depletion are anticipated to contribute an additional lifetime risk of skin cancer of four to 10 percent in children alive today," according to the Ultraviolet Measurements and Impacts Review Group, an independent review panel.
Its report is the first independent assessment of the impact of ozone depletion in Britain.

A companion report by the Stratospheric Ozone Review Group said losses of ozone over the Antarctic and Arctic had been significant earlier this year and said the problem would get worse before it got better.
The international community agreed in Montreal in 1987 to phase out production of chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and some other ozone-depleting substances.
The agreement, signed by 150 governments, should lead to the start of a recovery of the ozone layer in the next decade.
"Even so, the continuing damage caused to the ozone layer by man's activities will not be resolved for many decades, leading to an enhancement of UV radiation," the government said.
Environment Secretary John Gummer said the new scientific assessments underscored the importance of action taken by the European Union, which banned production of CFCs in 1995.
"There is no room for complacency and we will be working hard to achieve rapid reductions in ozone-depleting substances globally," Gummer said in a statement.

Governments are due to meet in Costa Rica later this month to decide on contributions by rich countries to developing nations to help them phase out use of ozone-depleting substances in line with the Montreal Protocol.

"This is a global problem, and it is not sufficient to eliminate production in developed countries -- we look to developing nations to play their part in eventually ridding the world of these destructive substances," Gummer said.
